newsitem.title: CANADA: Evacuees trickle home from Manitoba flood.
newsitem.headline: Evacuees trickle home from Manitoba flood.

text.p: Life began returning to normal in flood-stricken southern Manitoba on Wednesday as evacuees trickled home and the Red River's crest pushed north of Winnipeg.
"It'll be a relief to get back. Home is home," south Winnipeg evacuee Peter Tataryn said.

Tataryn was among the first of the 8,800 evacuated Winnipeggers to be allowed back home starting on Thursday, with most allowed back in the next two weeks. Manitoba's capital and largest city has 650,000 residents.

"I've lived here for 20 years. Obviously hindsight is 20/20 but if I was to do it over again, I wouldn't build in some of these areas," Winnipeg City Councillor John Angus told local television. Twenty-nine homes in the city flooded.
Angus said residents would be encouraged to build permanent dikes along the Red River where the riverbank was stable enough to support additional weight.
More than 28,000 Canadians and 50,000 Americans have been forced from their homes by the worst flooding since 1852. Four Canadians died due to the flood, police said.
The floods devastated southern Manitoba and North Dakota, causing more than $1 billion in damage and covering more than 800 square miles (2,072 sq km) of Canadian farmland.

About 600 people were allowed to return to the towns of Letellier and Dominion City about 10 miles (17 km) north of the U.S.-Canada border on Tuesday. But flood waters were still too high to allow the 1,700 residents of Morris to return home. Morris is about 22 miles north (35 km) of Letellier.

"We have booklets covering subjects such as how to determine if your home is safe, restoring utilities, clean-up and flood proofing and how to deal with stress following a flood," Manitoba Emergency Management coordinator Harold Clayton said.
Winds from the north were forecast to gust up to 45 mph (70 kmh) and thunder showers should drop 0.4 inch (10 mm) on Manitoba's Red River Valley later on Wednesday.
"Ten millimetres of rain would have little effect at this point, but 25 mm (1 inch) would delay the decline of the river," Manitoba Natural Resources flood liaison engineer Larry Whitney said.

Dikes in Canada's flood-ravaged Red River Valley were lashed since Monday by high winds and waves up to two feet (60 cm) high on the "Red Sea," an expanse of floodwater twice the size of Hong Kong. Defenses held without any major breaches.

The 29-mile (47-km) Floodway around Winnipeg's eastern edge was credited with sparing the city an estimated C$2 billion ($1.5 billion) in damage by keeping the Red River's peak level 10 feet (3 metres) lower at the city center.
The ditch was built after a quarter of Winnipeg's residents were evacuated in the smaller flood of 1950. The current flood is the third worst on record after floods in 1852 and 1826, Whitney said.
"We probably would have seen evacuations in the hundreds of thousands," Whitney said.
Grand Forks, N.D., was overwhelmed by the Red River on April 19 when 90 percent of its 50,000 residents fled rising water.
"Grand Forks was a troubling sight for us all. Consider four or five Grand Forks within our perimeter highway (beltway)," Whitney said.
